newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Central African Republic peace blueprint unveiled.
newsitem.headline: Central African Republic peace blueprint unveiled.

text.p: African mediators announced on Saturday agreement on a blueprint for peace in the Central African Republic designed as a lasting settlement following the impoverished nation's third army mutiny in under a year.
The draft calls for a national unity government and African peacekeepers.

French troops, in the former French colony under a defence pact, patrol the capital and form a buffer between mutineers and their foes in the presidential guard. France has welcomed the use of African peacekeepers.

Malian general Amadou Toumani Toure said at a ceremony after a week of round-table reconciliation talks that he would brief the presidents of Chad, Gabon, Burkina Faso and Mali and ask them to come to Bangui to sign the blueprint draft.
"We have weighed the vital need for a broad-based and open government of national unity in which a desire to work hard, for impartiality and sincerity are the cardinal virtues," he said.
"The possible and desirable presence of African forces is a mark of solidarity, of a commitment from our continent for a durable solution in the Central African Republic," he added.
The blueprint also called for the revival of a political protocol and a government programme agreed after the second mutiny in May.
Toumani Toure paid tribute to the mutineers for their openness to dialogue during the mediation process but did not specify their role in the eventual peace settlement.
Mutinies in April and May began over pay and conditions but turned into a campaign to oust Ange-Felix Patasse, a northern civilian politician who won presidential elections in 1993.
The latest mutiny, which began on November 15, degenerated into ethnic feuding. The overall death toll runs into hundreds.
A truce between mutineers, mainly minority Yakomas from the south, and army loyalists, expires on January 23.
Earlier, Toumani Toure said the four heads of state would travel to Bangui for the signing some time before January 23.

The four presidents -- Omar Bongo of Gabon, Alpha Oumar Konare of Mali, Blaise Compaore of Burkina Faso and Idriss Deby of Chad -- visited Bangui and launched the mediation bid at the request of a Franco-African summit in Burkina Faso in December.

Committees grouping all political parties and representatives of religious groups and society at large took part in the round-table talks and made recommendations on security, social and political issues and reconciliation.
Toumani Toure, who toppled Mali's former dictator Moussa Traore in 1991, is widely respected for the way he ushered in democracy in Mali a year later and then stepped down.

The Central African Republic hit world headlines in the 1970s with the extravagent rule of self-proclaimed emperor jean-Bedel Bokassa, who was toppled in a French-backed coup in 1979 and died last year.
